abstract.text: This paper studies spurious regressions in econometrics, showing that high R² with low Durbin-Watson can arise in independent nonstationary/autocorrelated time series and that standard significance tests are invalid. It uses simulations of random walks and ARIMA processes to quantify false rejection rates and recommends differencing or modeling levels and changes with attention to residual autocorrelation.

evidence.quote: From our own studies we would conclude that if a regression equation relating economic variables is found to have strongly autocorrelated residuals, equivalent to a low Durbin-Watson value, the onZy conclusion that can be reached is that the equation is mis-specified, whatever the value of R2 observed.

thesis.text: Regressions between nonstationary or highly autocorrelated economic time series can appear highly significant with high R² and low Durbin-Watson values even when the series are independent, so such equations are often spurious and their usual significance tests invalid.

There is thus a good deal of evidence to suggest that the appropriate value for d in eq. (4) is very often one. [See, for example, Granger (1966), Reid (1969) and Newbold and Granger (1974).]

Such models are often employed as bench-marks against which the forecast performance of econometric models can be judged. [For a criticism of this approach to evaluation, see Granger and Newbold (1973).]
To put these results in context, they may be compared with results reported by Malinvaud (1966).

As an example (admittedly extreme) of the changes that can occur in one’s results from differencing, Sheppard (197 1) regressed U.K. consumption on autonomous expenditure and mid-year money stock, both for levels and changes for the time period 1947-1962.

One method we are currently considering is to build single series models for each variable, using the methods of Box and Jenkins (1970) for example, and then searching for relationships between series by relating the residuals from these single models.

sections.summary: Reviews stationary ARMA/ARIMA models and differencing, argues economic series are often highly autocorrelated and need d=1 or near-unit-root specifications, and gives random walk and integrated moving average examples.
sections.title: Time-series models and nonstationary economic series

sections.summary: Sets up the standard regression model and F test, shows the null distribution breaks under autocorrelated/nonstationary Y, and uses Kendall's variance result to argue high R² can occur between independent autocorrelated series.
sections.title: How nonsense regressions can arise: theory

source_span.end_text: Our second simulation was more comprehensive.

sections.summary: First simulation of two independent random walks of length 50 shows the t-test rejects about three-quarters of the time; variance is underestimated by a factor of about 5.6. A second simulation varies m=1–5 and series types.
sections.title: Simulation evidence for independent random walks and multiple regressors

source_span.start_text: Our second simulation was more comprehensive.

sections.summary: Reports that for random walks and ARIMA(0,1,1) levels, rejection probability becomes very small for m>3; white-noise changes are satisfactory, but changes in ARIMA(0,1,1) reject twice as often. High R² with low d is no indication of a true relationship.
sections.title: Interpreting the simulations: spurious relationships are the rule

sections.summary: Argues autocorrelated residuals imply mis-specification regardless of R²; recommends first differences for highly autocorrelated variables and building models with both levels and changes; discusses theory, structural models, and R² testing.
sections.title: Discussion and recommendations: mis-specification, differencing, and model building

corrections.value_json: "First simulation of two independent random walks of length 50 shows the t-test rejects about three-quarters of the time; the standard deviation of the slope coefficient is underestimated by a factor of about 5.6. A second simulation varies m=1–5 and series types."
corrections.reason: The paper states that the standard deviation (not the variance) of the slope estimate is underestimated by a factor of about 5.6; the variance factor is (5.6)² ≈ 31.4. The draft misreports this as the variance being underestimated by 5.6.

evidence.quote: In fact, the observed average value of S was 4.5, suggesting that the standard deviation of & is being underestimated by the multiple factor 5.6.
our simulation indicates that the estimated variance of fll should be multiplied by (5.6)” N 31.4 when T = 50 and random walks are involved.

corrections.value_json: "Reports that for random walks and ARIMA(0,1,1) levels, the probability of accepting H0 becomes very small for m>3; white-noise changes are satisfactory, but changes in ARIMA(0,1,1) reject twice as often. High R² with low d is no indication of a true relationship."
corrections.reason: The paper reports that the probability of ACCEPTING H0 becomes very small for m>3 (i.e. rejection becomes near-certain, matching table 2's 93–96% rejections); the draft inverts this to 'rejection probability becomes very small'.

evidence.quote: It is seen that the probability of accepting H,, the hypothesis of no relationship, becomes very small indeed for m > 3 when regressions involve indepen-
dent random walks.
